notes: A field contributor explains mathematical results and their limits; the survey is selective rather than exhaustive.
Connects nonlinear mathematics, biological timing, physical order and engineered networks; production and institutional layers are thinner.
Coupling and collective behaviour transfer well, but much underlying physics will be familiar to this reader.
Explains how synchronisation arises and fails, without the mathematical detail of a specialist treatment.
Examples advance the common mechanism; research portraits create some narrative overhead.
The main mechanisms and research history remain durable.
Applied mathematics, physical models and networks fit directly.
Direct research authority and serious mathematical reception justify full authority attainment.
A clear progression from living to physical and exploratory systems.
Controlled explanations distinguish intuition from mathematical detail.
books.case: The mathematical-reader review identifies a coherent bridge between very different synchronising systems and a useful account of research itself. It is a stronger intellectual fit than a generic physics introduction. The central limitation is that explanations aimed at broad readers provide less new technical and industrial insight for an experienced theoretical physicist.
books.objection: A common mathematical phenomenon across many examples is not the same as integrating production, institutions and economic constraints.
books.eligibility: Narrative popular mathematics, not a textbook, problem course or technical reference. No serious veto is established. A desired-profile example is assessed by the same gates as every other nomination.
books.theme: The central subject is synchronisation, not disease, ecology or philosophy. T11=T12=0. Scientific history serves a cross-period explanation, so H13=0. P14 uses the original 2003 work, not the 2004 paperback.

reviews: Robert W. Hayden, Mathematical Association of America
notes: Substantial research and references, but a mathematical reviewer identifies minor technical errors and vagueness.
Connects inference, computing, scientific institutions and operational applications across fields.
The history of adoption transfers; the mathematical method will add less for an experienced modeller.
Some application stories show why inference helped, but technical explanation is uneven.
A coherent narrative with considerable personality and controversy material.
History of inference and its institutional acceptance is durable.
Probability, computing and strategic estimation are directly relevant.
Careful science journalism with specialist attention, below direct methodological authority.
Engaging historical narrative and readable application stories.
Technical imprecision and occasionally dramatic opposition narratives reduce precision.
books.case: This is a history of Bayesian ideas in practice, rather than training in Bayesian computation. Zeger values its connections to real applications. Hayden's independent mathematical review is more reserved about technical explanation and identifies errors and vague passages. Those reservations matter for this reader even though the history remains worthwhile.
books.objection: An engaging history of a method cannot substitute for a deep explanation of the method's limits; the apparent conflict between rival statistical camps can also become too neat.
books.eligibility: A general-reader explanatory history passes the hard exclusions. No serious central epistemic failure or other veto is established from the local weaknesses reported by the reviewers.
books.theme: Statistics is the central topic; war, intelligence, medicine and elections are applications. T11=T12=0. The account spans several centuries of an evolving method rather than one central bounded episode, so H13=0. P14 uses 2011, not the 2012 paperback.

reviews: Ian Bright, Society of Professional Economists
Tim Denvir, BCS FACS Facts, pages 63–64
notes: Explicit treatment of uncertainty, evidence quality and model limits; the subjective-probability position remains an argued view.
Links statistical inference, forecasting, communication and institutional decisions, with less industrial-system integration.
Useful risk-communication and calibration lessons; basic probability is familiar to this reader.
Explains sources of uncertainty and how evidence changes a judgment; not every case supplies a complete causal model.
Most cases advance the argument; some historical and everyday examples are less efficient for an expert.
Uncertainty representation and model humility remain useful beyond the examples.
Quantification, modelling and strategic risk are direct fits.
Leading statistician with direct work on public risk communication and specialist scrutiny.
Chapter structure and summaries make a demanding argument navigable.
Precise distinctions and worked examples support controlled prose.
books.case: The strongest contribution is disciplined treatment of what a number does and does not tell us. Reviews by professional economists and computing specialists connect its lessons to forecasting and communication. The book's difficulty is not itself a density defect; its lower utility mark reflects the user's existing mathematical expertise.
books.objection: A wide survey of uncertainty does not necessarily give a physicist much new mathematics or a complete account of industrial and institutional systems.
books.eligibility: A sustained explanatory account for general readers, not a technical statistics course or a procedural manual. Philosophical questions support the statistical argument rather than defining an independent philosophical treatise. No serious veto established.
books.theme: Statistical uncertainty is central; finance, health, policy and philosophical definitions are applications or foundations. T11=T12=0; this classification has moderate confidence. H13=0. P14 uses the UK original in 2024, not the US release in 2025.
